statement: In the world's population aged 15 and older, as modelled in two Global Burden of Disease (GBD) analyses, the second an update of the first that keeps 17 of its curves, drinking compared with not drinking is associated with a combined risk of 22 or 23 alcohol-linked diseases and injuries (each weighted by its share of the population's ill health, measured in disability-adjusted life years, DALYs) that is lowest at or near zero for people aged 15 to 39, and at about half a standard drink (10 g of ethanol) a day for people aged 40 and older: these are model estimates resting on relative-risk curves fitted to observational studies of self-reported drinking, and every lowest point above zero comes from lower risks of ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes in those studies (editors' reading of how the models are built), which genetic studies mostly do not find. In GBD 2016 (Griswold et al., 2018), one curve weighted by the world's 2016 disease mix had its lowest point at 0 standard drinks a day (95% uncertainty interval 0 to 0.8 a day; the abstract prints it per week) and rose with intake; of its 23 conditions only ischaemic heart disease had a significant dip (lowest relative risk 0.86 in men at 0.83 drinks a day and 0.82 in women at 0.92), diabetes and ischaemic stroke dipped non-significantly, and the risks of all the others, every cancer among them, rose with intake; in women the lower heart disease and diabetes risks were offset mainly by cancers. In GBD 2020 (Bryazka et al., 2022), with weights from each region's, age group's and sex's own disease mix, the lowest point at ages 15 to 39 was 0 to 0.603 drinks a day across regions (worldwide 0.136 for men and 0.273 for women), and the combined risk was back at a non-drinker's level at 0.249 drinks a day for men and 0.546 for women worldwide (about 2.5 and 5.5 g; editors' arithmetic), injuries, whose risk rose with intake, making up much of the ill health weighed at these ages (66.3% in men, 47.9% in women); at 40 to 64 the lowest point was 0.527 (men) and 0.562 (women) drinks a day and the non-drinker level was reached at 1.69 and 1.82; at 65 and older, 0.636 and 0.656, and 3.19 and 3.51. Differences between women and men were not significant. Worldwide and age-standardised, the 2020 lowest point was 0.511 (0.400 to 0.700) drinks a day, and 0.534 (0 to 1.00) when the 2016 curves were given the 2020 weights, so the move away from zero comes mostly from the weights (editors' reading). The lowest-risk amount is the bottom of an average of many curves for a whole population, not one person's risk and not a risk-free amount; drinking a lot on some days was not modelled, alcohol use disorder, depression, anxiety and dementia were left out of the 2020 curves, and the authors expect that including the last three would lower the amounts. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Two world models by one research team added up the risks of 22 or 23 diseases and injuries linked to alcohol, each counted by how much illness it causes. For people aged 15 to 39, the overall risk was lowest at no alcohol or almost none, and it was back at a non-drinker's level by about a quarter of a 10-gram drink a day for men and half a drink for women. For people aged 40 and over, the newer model put the lowest risk at about half a drink a day, because some studies link small amounts to less heart disease, stroke and diabetes; most studies using genes did not find this for heart disease and diabetes. The lowest-risk amount is not a no-risk amount: the risk of every cancer rose with drinking. The models describe whole populations, not one person, and did not look at drinking a lot on some days.
population: The world's population aged 15 and older as modelled: 195 locations, 1990 to 2016 (GBD 2016), and GBD regions by 5-year age group and sex, 1990 to 2020 (GBD 2020)
exposure: Average daily alcohol intake, in standard drinks of 10 g of ethanol (curves fitted for 0 to 12.5 drinks a day in 2016, sampled from 0 to 100 g a day in 2020); current drinking means at least one drink in the past 12 months
comparator: Not drinking: the non-drinking groups of the underlying studies, whose make-up varied (in 2016 adjusted for former drinkers only for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes; in 2020 through bias covariates chosen by the model)
outcome: A combined, DALY-weighted risk of 23 (2016) or 22 (2020) alcohol-linked conditions, including heart disease, stroke, diabetes, cancers, tuberculosis and injuries: the intake at which it is lowest (theoretical minimum risk exposure level, TMREL) and, in 2020, the intake at which it is back at a non-drinker's level (non-drinker equivalence, NDE)
magnitude: GBD 2016 (Griswold et al., 2018; 23 outcomes, 592 studies, 3,992 relative-risk estimates; one curve weighted by global age-standardised 2016 DALY rates, both sexes; standard drink 10 g): lowest point of the weighted curve 0 standard drinks a day (95% UI 0.0 to 0.8 a day; printed per week in the abstract), rising monotonically; ischaemic heart disease lowest relative risk 0.86 (0.80 to 0.96) in men at 0.83 drinks a day and 0.82 (0.72 to 0.95) in women at 0.92; non-significant dips for diabetes and ischaemic stroke; all cancers rising. GBD 2020 (Bryazka et al., 2022; 22 curves, five re-fitted with 71 more studies; weights by region, age, sex and year; TMREL the lowest point, NDE the return to a non-drinker's risk; standard drinks a day): all populations, TMREL 0 (0 to 0) to 1.87 (0.500 to 3.30); ages 15 to 39 across regions TMREL 0 to 0.603 (0.400 to 1.00), NDE 0.002 (0 to 0) to 1.75 (0.698 to 4.30); global males TMREL 0.136 (0 to 0.400), NDE 0.249 (0 to 1.00), females 0.273 (0 to 0.500) and 0.546 (0 to 1.30); ages 40 to 64, males 0.527 (0.400 to 1.00) and 1.69 (0.800 to 3.20), females 0.562 (0.400 to 0.800) and 1.82 (1.00 to 3.10); 65 and older, males 0.636 (0.500 to 1.00) and 3.19 (1.50 to 5.20), females 0.656 (0.500 to 1.00) and 3.51 (1.70 to 5.50); ages 40 and older across regions, TMREL 0.114 (0 to 0.403) to 1.87 (0.500 to 3.30), NDE 0.193 (0 to 0.900) to 6.94 (3.40 to 8.30). Global, age-standardised, both sexes: GBD 2016 0 (0 to 0.800); GBD 2016 curves with 2020 weights 0.534 (0 to 1.00), NDE 0.669 (0 to 1.40); GBD 2020 0.511 (0.400 to 0.700), NDE 1.72 (0.80 to 3.30). Hypothetical curves for alcohol use disorders and alcoholic cardiomyopathy lowered the TMREL by 0.058 to 0.146 drinks a day on average. In grams (editors' arithmetic, 10 g a drink): 0.249 drinks is about 2.5 g, 0.546 about 5.5 g, 0.511 about 5.1 g.

evidence.extracted: The minimum of the DALY-weighted curve over all attributable outcomes (the theoretical minimum risk exposure level) was zero standard drinks a day (95% UI 0.0 to 0.8 drinks a day; the abstract prints the interval per week), and the weighted risk rose monotonically with intake; the protective associations for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes in females were offset mainly by cancers. Weights were each outcome's global age-standardised DALY rate per 100,000 in 2016, both sexes; curves were fitted for 0 to 12.5 standard drinks a day; a covariate for former drinkers in the reference group was kept only for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes. In a sensitivity analysis of the weights, the curve changed significantly only where diabetes and ischaemic heart disease made up more than 60% of deaths.

evidence.extracted: Relative risks for 23 outcomes came from 3,992 estimates in 592 prospective and retrospective studies (about 28 million people); exposure from 694 sources; 195 locations, ages 15 to 95 and older. A standard drink is 10 g of ethanol; current drinking is at least one drink in the past 12 months. Uncertainty intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 1000 draws carrying sampling error and modelling uncertainty from hyper-parameter selection and parameter estimation. The authors list as limitations that drinking patterns were not modelled, unrecorded consumption may be missed, people under 15 were not assessed and outcomes such as dementia were left out. Funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

evidence.locator: Methods › Estimating dose–response relative risks, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Methods › Estimating TMREL and NDE, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: GBD 2020 re-reviewed the six outcomes with the most alcohol-attributable DALYs with 71 additional studies, dropped lower respiratory infection and used 22 relative-risk curves (five re-fitted, 17 carried over from GBD 2016), relative to non-drinkers and sampled from 0 to 100 g a day. The theoretical minimum risk exposure level (TMREL) and the non-drinker equivalence (NDE, the intake at which the weighted risk again equals a non-drinker's) come from a weighted average of the curves, each cause weighted by its share of DALYs (years of life lost plus years lived with disability) in each region, age, sex and year. Across all regions, ages, sexes and years the 2020 TMREL ranged from 0 (0 to 0) to 1.87 (0.500 to 3.30) standard drinks (10 g) a day; TMREL and NDE varied significantly by age but not by sex or year. Editors' reading of the methods: one curve per cause is applied to every region, so differences between populations come from their mix of diseases.

evidence.extracted: Citing a systematic review of Mendelian randomization studies (van de Luitgaarden et al., 2021), the discussion reports that 67% of such studies of cardiovascular disease and 75% of those of diabetes found no association with alcohol, and that only five of 24 tested a non-linear relationship. Stated limitations: drinking patterns not modelled; alcohol use disorders excluded from the TMREL; possible residual confounding, selection bias, measurement bias and reverse causation in the relative risks; self-reported intake; weights that include DALYs caused by alcohol; depression, anxiety and dementia not included, which would probably lower the TMREL and NDE. Hypothetical curves for alcohol use disorders and alcoholic cardiomyopathy lowered the TMREL on average by 0.058 (0.00 to 0.30), 0.092 (0.00 to 0.50) and 0.146 (0.00 to 0.60) standard drinks a day in three scenarios. Funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

evidence.locator: Title; Comment, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Declaration of interests
evidence.extracted: A comment published with GBD 2016 states in its title that no level of alcohol consumption improves health. It restates the minimum-risk level as 0 g of ethanol a week, without its interval, presented as the level minimising an individual's risk, and explains it by lower ischaemic heart disease and diabetes risks in women being cancelled out by cancer risks that rise steadily with intake; it calls the conclusions unambiguous and takes them as strong support for the UK Chief Medical Officers' guideline that there is no safe level of drinking. Both authors were employed by Public Health England. Its figures are second-hand from GBD 2016.

risk_of_bias.note: The curves are fitted to observational studies of self-reported intake; GBD 2016 describes no appraisal of its 592 studies and allowed for former drinkers in the reference group only for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes; GBD 2020 chose bias covariates by a Lasso, with the sets in an appendix not read; the dips at low intake that produce every non-zero lowest point are where confounding and abstainer bias are most disputed (editors' checklist high on cards sc_griswold_2018 and sc_bryazka_2022).

inconsistency.note: The two analyses differ on the worldwide figure (0 against 0.511 drinks a day), a difference explained by the change of weights (0.534 with the 2016 curves and 2020 weights); they agree for ages 15 to 39.

indirectness.note: A population-weighted average of curves stands in for the question a person asks; one curve per condition is applied to every region; drinking patterns, several conditions and people under 15 are left out; the 'non-drinkers' of the 2020 curves are not defined in the main text.

imprecision.note: Intervals are narrow at older ages and wide for young adults (NDE 0 to 1.00 drinks a day for men aged 15 to 39) and do not include the choice of weights or of conditions; these limits are counted under risk of bias and indirectness rather than twice.

grade.reasoning: The model outputs are not graded as evidence of an effect; the claim is graded from the evidence behind the curves, observational cohort and case-control studies, which starts low and is rated down for risk of bias and indirectness: very low. Worded as an association in modelled populations: these analyses cannot show that alcohol makes the combined risk rise or fall at any amount, and a lowest-risk amount is a property of a weighted average for a population, not a safe amount for a person. Genetic (Mendelian randomization) studies, cited here second-hand through the 2020 discussion, use gene variants linked to drinking, which addresses some confounding, but effects of the variants through other routes (pleiotropy), weak instruments, selection (for example analyses split by drinking status) and the inability of most to show a curve at low intake remain; they concern heart disease and diabetes, are rated in the answers on the heart, and are not used to raise or lower this rating. Overlapping evidence: GBD 2016 and GBD 2020 are one group's analyses sharing 17 of 22 curves, and the comment (Burton & Sheron, 2018) restates GBD 2016 and adds no data, so the agreement for young people is not independent replication. Status contested: the 2016 zero, read in the accompanying comment as showing that no level of drinking improves health, and the 2020 J-shaped curves at 40 and older point different ways, and the genetic evidence the 2020 authors cite is a credible critique of the dips that produce every non-zero lowest point.

debate.question: Is there an amount of alcohol that adds no risk to health, or does any amount add some risk?
debate.evidence_yes: The 2020 model (Bryazka et al., 2022; sc_bryazka_2022; funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation), which weighted the curves by each population's own mix of diseases, found the combined risk lowest above zero at ages 40 and older: about half a standard drink a day worldwide (0.527 to 0.656), and not back at a non-drinker's level until 1.69 to 3.51 drinks a day; across regions the lowest point at these ages ran from 0.114 (0 to 0.403) to 1.87 (0.500 to 3.30) drinks a day, and the abstract calls the curve J-shaped in every region. Worldwide and age-standardised, the lowest point was 0.511 (0.400 to 0.700) drinks a day, and the 2016 curves gave 0.534 with the 2020 weights, so the 2016 zero did not survive a change of weights; the 2016 model's own interval already reached 0.8 drinks a day (Griswold et al., 2018; sc_griswold_2018; funded by the same foundation). The dip comes from observational findings: in the 2016 review ischaemic heart disease had a significant dip at low intake (lowest relative risk 0.86 in men and 0.82 in women at about 0.8 to 0.9 drinks a day), with non-significant dips for diabetes and ischaemic stroke. The cohort evidence on deaths from any cause is in the answer on living longer.
debate.evidence_no: In the 2016 model the combined risk for the world's population rose steadily from zero: the lower heart disease and diabetes risks seen in women were outweighed, mainly by cancers, and the risk of every cancer rose with intake (Griswold et al., 2018). A comment published with it said in its title that no level of drinking improves health and took the result as strong support for the UK Chief Medical Officers' guideline that there is no safe level (Burton & Sheron, 2018; sc_burton_2018; both authors then employed by Public Health England; its figures are second-hand). The 2020 model agrees for younger people: at 15 to 39 the lowest point ran from 0 to 0.603 drinks a day across regions, and worldwide the combined risk was back at a non-drinker's level by 0.249 drinks a day for men and 0.546 for women (about 2.5 and 5.5 g; editors' arithmetic), injuries making up 66.3% of the ill health from the 22 conditions in young men. Every lowest point above zero comes from the dips for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes (editors' reading of how the models are built), and the 2020 authors report that most genetic studies found no association of alcohol with heart and blood-vessel disease (67%) or diabetes (75%) (Bryazka et al., 2022). The 2020 curves leave out alcohol use disorder, alcohol-related heart muscle disease, depression, anxiety and dementia; hypothetical curves for the first two lowered the lowest point by 0.058 to 0.146 drinks a day on average, and the authors expect the last three would lower it too.
debate.neither_can_show: Any one person's risk: the curves average many conditions weighted by a whole population's disease mix, with one curve per condition applied to every region. Whether alcohol causes the differences: the curves are fitted to observational studies of self-reported drinking, whose non-drinking groups vary and were adjusted for former drinkers only for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes in 2016, and in which the 2020 authors name residual confounding, selection bias and reverse causation as possible. Drinking patterns: drinking a lot on some days was modelled in neither analysis. How uncertain the amounts are: the intervals carry sampling and model-parameter uncertainty but are not said to include the choice of weights or of conditions (editors' observation), and the worldwide figure moved from 0 to 0.534 with the same curves when only the weights changed. Independence: both analyses come from one research group and share 17 of the 22 curves, so their agreement for young people is not independent replication.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In both models, for people aged 15 to 39 the combined risk is lowest at or near zero and is back at a non-drinker's level within about a quarter (men) to half (women) of a 10-g drink a day worldwide, so these models find at most a very small dip for young adults. For people aged 40 and older, the 2020 model puts the lowest combined risk at about half a drink a day, but only because of lower heart disease, stroke and diabetes risks in observational studies, which genetic studies mostly do not find; if those dips come from bias, the lowest point would be zero at every age (editors' reading of how the models are built). A lowest-risk amount is not a risk-free amount: it is where the model's gains and losses across conditions balance best for a whole population, and in the 2016 curves the risk of every cancer rose with intake. Neither model looked at drinking a lot on some days, and neither is a guide to one person's risk.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Dose-response curves for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes at low intake from designs less open to confounding and abstainer bias, above all genetic studies able to show a curve, in large cohorts of several ancestries that separate people who never drank from former drinkers; data on drinking patterns; and weights fixed in advance and published with all sensitivity analyses, with the combined curves checked against deaths from all causes in populations with different mixes of disease. None of the sources read reports these.
